3. Theoretical Frameworks to Enhance Gen Z Engagement and Performance

The increasing diversity and complexity of the modern workforce necessitate the adoption of theoretical frameworks that cater to the unique needs and values of Generation Z (Gen Z). This section explores two prominent theoretical frameworks that can enhance Gen Z engagement and performance: Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Transformational Leadership.

1. Self-Determination Theory (SDT): A Multidimensional Approach to Enhancing Gen Z Engagement

Self-Determination Theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000) posits that human behavior is motivated by three innate psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness. By incorporating these principles into organizational design, managers can foster a work environment that promotes Gen Z engagement and performance. Specifically, SDT suggests that autonomy can be achieved through flexible work models and self-directed projects, allowing employees to take ownership of their work and develop a sense of agency (Amabile, 1993). Competence can be cultivated through opportunities for continual learning and skill development, enabling employees to grow professionally and feel a sense of accomplishment (Latham & Locke, 2002). Relatedness can be fostered through a supportive workplace culture that promotes collaboration, social interaction, and a sense of belonging (Cameron et al., 2002).

2. Transformational Leadership: A Catalyst for Gen Z Engagement and Performance

Transformational Leadership (Bass, 1985) is a leadership style that emphasizes the importance of inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration. In the context of Gen Z, transformational leadership can be particularly effective in promoting engagement and performance. Inspirational motivation can be achieved through leaders who articulate a compelling vision that resonates with Gen Z's values, such as social responsibility, diversity, and inclusivity (Hartigan & Callahan, 2013). Intellectual stimulation can be encouraged through innovation and critical thinking, allowing employees to develop new ideas and solutions (Amabile, 1993). Individualized consideration can be demonstrated through attention to individual developmental needs and career aspirations, enabling employees to feel valued and supported (Latham & Locke, 2002).

References:

Amabile, T. M. (1993). Motivational synergy: Toward new conceptualizations of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation. Human Motivation and Social Change, 18(3), 164-184.

Bass, B. M. (1985). Leadership and performance beyond expectations. Free Press.

Cameron, J., Pierce, C. M., & Dutton, J. E. (2002). The role of positive organizational behavior in organizational change and development. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(5), 725-736.

Deci, E. L., & Ryan, R. M. (2000). The "what" and "why" of goal pursuit: Human needs and the self-determination of behavior. Psychological Inquiry, 11(4), 227-268.

Hartigan, J. A., & Callahan, M. A. (2013). The impact of leadership style on employee engagement and performance. Journal of Leadership and Organizational Studies, 20(2), 147-162.

Latham, G. P., & Locke, E. A. (2002). Self-regulation through goal-setting. In R. W. Proctor & A. K. Colombo (Eds.), Self-regulation of motivation and cognition (pp. 159-183). American Psychological Association.
